answer_json.answer: Being left out of the move

lesson_text: Being left out. FOMO is the fear of missing out, and in trading it's the fear of missing a move. Something exciting is happening, you're on the sidelines, and you feel like you have to be in it right now. Notice it's not fear of losing. It's fear of a gain you don't have. That's what makes it dangerous. It pushes you to buy fast, with no plan, often after the move. FOMO wants you in right now, on somebody else's move.

choices: Being left out of the move

lesson_text: True, that's a chase. You came in late, after the move already happened, and paid up for it. Here's what it costs you. Your stop's still down where the idea is wrong, so you're further from it. More risk on every share. And you're often buying from the people who got in early, sometimes right as it's ready to turn. Come in that late and there's not much left for you. If the move already ran without you, paying up for it is a chase.

answer_json.answer: Your risk per share got bigger

lesson_text: Your risk per share got bigger. Risk per share is your entry minus your stop. The stop didn't move, your entry did, so the gap between them grew. Keep your normal share count and you're now risking more dollars than you planned. That's how a chase quietly blows up your risk. The fix: keep the dollar risk the same and buy fewer shares. And past 4% above the buy point, we don't buy it at all. Every dollar you chase gets added to your risk per share.

answer_json.answer: Loss aversion, a loss hits harder

lesson_text: Loss aversion. Same $500 either way, but the loss is the one you feel. Most people are wired like that. A loss stings more than a gain of the same size feels good. At the screen, that sting pulls you off your plan. You skip good triggers. You sit on losers, because taking the loss makes it real. Being careful with risk is fine, that's just risk aversion. Loss aversion is the lopsided part, and the plan is how you beat it. Your gut weighs a loss heavier than a gain. Let the plan do the weighing.

lesson_text: Write it down before the open. For every planned buy, put down the entry, the stop and the size before the bell. We do it on every trade. Then the trigger isn't a decision anymore. You made it already, calm, with the chart in front of you. At the trigger you just carry it out. Better yet, have the order staged so one click does it. The freeze lives in that moment of deciding under pressure. Take the deciding out of the moment and there's nothing left to freeze on. Decide before the open. At the trigger, you just carry it out.

reveal_json.lesson_line: Warm up the trader, not just the watchlist.
reveal_json.simple: True, because a warm-up gets your head ready too, not just your charts.
reveal_json.why: True. The charts are half the job. You're the other half. Before the bell I want to know what kind of head I'm in. Tired, still mad about yesterday's loss, or bored and itching to press buttons. Name the problem most likely to hit you today and decide how you'll handle it. A clean watchlist doesn't help much if the person trading it is on tilt, trading off emotion instead of the plan.

lesson_text: Entry, stop and size, for every name. Every buy we make has those three written down before the market opens. At the open things move fast. You don't want to be doing math with your finger on the button. Decide the trigger, the stop and the share count while you're calm, then set an alert at each trigger. Now the open is just execution. It doesn't mean you buy all five. It means nothing gets bought without a plan. Every name on today's list gets its levels before the bell.

lesson_text: Practice, prep and review. Look at the fields where people perform under pressure, like sport, music and chess. The best spend more time practising and preparing than performing. Trading's the same. A new indicator is still you reading it, and a tip is someone else's read. The reps are what build you: prep before the open, trade the plan, review the film after. Nobody sells discipline. You build it. Train like an athlete: prep, perform, review. Better tools don't replace the reps.

lesson_text: The right moves become automatic. That's the whole point of a routine. Find what you do well, then repeat it until you can't not do it. Writing the plan, setting the stop, taking the loss when it's hit. When those run on autopilot, you stop burning energy fighting yourself. It doesn't mean you stop feeling things. You'll still feel fear and greed. The habits just carry you through it. Repeat the right steps until you don't need the checklist.

lesson_text: Earnings dates and overnight news. Check the date on every name. We don't buy in the 3 days before an earnings report. A report can gap a stock right past your stop overnight, and no stop can catch that. Then scan the overnight news. News outside market hours can open a stock far above or below where it closed, and your levels need to know that. Fed and CPI days are different. Know they're coming, but we trade them like any other day. Before the bell, know every name's earnings date and the overnight news.

answer_json.answer: A written if-then plan for it

lesson_text: Write an if-then plan for it. You already know how this one goes, so decide the answer now, while you're calm. Something like: if I take a loss and feel the itch to jump back in, then I stand up and take 15 minutes. If the setup triggers again, it's a new trade with its own stop. Write it down before the bell. In the moment, the sting of the loss argues louder than any good intention. A plan you made calm wins that argument. Know your pattern. Write the plan for it before the bell, not after the damage.

lesson_text: So you actually follow the plan when it's real. A plan made calm before the bell doesn't always survive a fast open. You're in a different head by then. Rehearsing closes that gap. You've already seen the early dump in your mind and already know what you'll do, so you just do it. Either you test the plan in rehearsal, or the market tests it with your money. And it's not a forecast. Running a few scenarios keeps you from marrying one. Rehearse the response before the bell, so the market isn't your first test.

lesson_text: False. A big high after a win can hurt you the same way a big low after a loss can. In a study of 80 day traders, the ones who reacted more intensely to gains and to losses traded significantly worse. It's one study, and it shows a link, not proof. But think about how it plays out. You hit a big winner, you feel bulletproof, and the next trade gets sloppy. That's also why we never raise risk past the rules after a run of winners. Feeling good is fine. Feeling invincible is the warning sign. Check in after big wins too. A big high is a warning sign, just like a big low.

answer_json.answer: Write it out, then set it aside

lesson_text: Write it out, then put it away. Grab a notebook and write for up to 15 minutes: what happened, how you feel, what you'll do about it later. Getting it on paper frees up the part of your head the market needs. Then it waits until after the close. If it's still eating at you at the open, that's a distracted day. Distracted means no new trades for us. Get it on paper, then draw a line under it. It waits until after the close.

prompt_json.q: Before the open
steps: Start with the game plan. Today's names, the levels, and an entry, stop and size for each one.
Then check the trader. How you slept, what's on your mind, which mistake is most likely to bite today.
Write an if-then for that mistake, like a 15-minute break when the urge hits. Commit to it before the bell.
Tired, sick, angry or distracted, and it's a no-new-trades day. That's part of the plan too.

prompt_json.q: During and after
steps: During the session, trade the plan. Take a short break before you're drained, not after.
After the close, write it up while it's fresh. What went well, what went wrong, what you'd do better.
Then pick one thing to work on tomorrow. One thing, and specific. Small steps every day add up.
